newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy shows signs of slowing -- S.F. Fed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy shows signs of slowing -- S.F. Fed.

text.p: The U.S. economy is showing signs it might be slowing to a more sustainable rate of growth, and such phenomenon may continue, said the head of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Robert Parry.

"What could help dampen inflationary pressures is if the economy were to slow to a more sustainable rate. As it turns out, we're seeing signs that it may be happening," Parry said at a Japan Society luncheon in Los Angeles.
"And there are reasons to expect a more sustainable growth rate to continue," Parry added.
A copy of Parry's speech was made available in New York.
Parry outlined a few factors which could contribute to the expected continuation of the economic slowdown. They were:
-- Strong dollar;
-- Moderately high interest rate levels;
-- Strong spending for real assets by businesses and consumers;
-- Restrained federal spending.
The San Francisco Fed president said the central bank's key concern now is whether the slowdown will be enough to avoid inflation.

"The key concern for Fed policymakers is whether that slowing ... will be enough to prevent an inflation problem from arising," Parry said, adding that the Fed remains committed to keeping price rises "under control."
Parry also said the U.S. economy was performing "extremely well," saying that the current strength was seen in "virtually all sectors of the economy."
Parry said the combination of economic strength and lower inflation "has contributed to strong demand in equity markets."

The San Francisco Fed chief said U.S. labor and product markets were likely to be tight. "Right now, labor and product markets appear to be tight, and traditionally, that pattern has spelled higher inflation," Parry said.
The Fed official said, however, that some factors -- such as a recent decelaration in employer's benefits costs and a strong dollar -- have contributed to keep inflation "quiescent."

But Parry said those factors currently holding inflation down might be transitory. "There are a couple of things that are helping to contain inflation today, but they'll probably have less and less effect as time goes on," he said.
Parry also said the U.S. might be seeing higher productivity due to technological enhancements.
"For the last five years, investment in the (technology) sector has been growing at double digit rates; in fact, it hit almost 20 percent last year," Parry said.
"So we may be seeing it pay off in productivity increases ... But it also matters whether this fundamental change is big enough to make that much of a difference," he addded.
(( -- Jose Paulo Vicente, 212-859-1676 ))
